# From Reservoir to Rooftop: How City Water Finds Its Way Up

Water is heavy. This single fact explains almost everything about how municipal water systems are designed. A column of water one foot tall exerts about 0.433 pounds per square inch (psi) of pressure at its base, which means that lifting water is fundamentally a fight against gravity, and every component of a city's water infrastructure—from the elevation of its reservoirs to the pumps in a downtown high-rise—is an engineering response to that fight.

## The Fundamental Principle: Elevation as Energy

The cheapest way to pressurize water is not to pump it at all, but to let gravity do the work. This is why cities historically built reservoirs on hills, and why modern systems place treated water in elevated storage tanks. The concept engineers use is called "hydraulic head": the energy contained in water by virtue of its elevation. Water at 200 feet above a faucet delivers roughly 86 psi at that faucet, before accounting for friction losses in the pipes. Municipal systems typically aim to deliver water to customers at pressures between about 40 and 80 psi, which corresponds to a useful elevation window of roughly 90 to 185 feet.
